content: Depending on the capabilities of basic healthcare facilities, some countries may choose to classify certain medicines as essential within their national plans. The Essential Trauma Care (EsTC) list of medicines is not exhaustive and does not include all medications that trauma patients might require. For example, antimalarial agents are extensively covered in the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines but are not addressed in the Guidelines for Essential Trauma Care. The Model List emphasizes that selecting medicines is only the first step, which must be followed by their appropriate and effective use. The WHO, through its Essential Drugs and Medicines program, provides consultation to countries to enhance their capacity to deliver essential medicines. Similar considerations may need to be addressed when developing essential trauma care systems. Certain medications, such as those for pain, fever, and inflammation (Section 2 of the Model List), are subject to international control under the United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (1988). These regulations can sometimes hinder access to the most effective analgesics, particularly in rural and low-income areas. Trauma patients, who often experience severe pain, represent one of the largest groups in need of effective and affordable pain relief. Medications listed in Sections 3 (Anaphylaxis) and 4 (Poisonings) of the Model List are included in trauma care guidelines due to their potential use in managing complications, such as allergic reactions to antibiotics or respiratory depression caused by narcotics. Under Section 6 (Infections), only antibiotics relevant to the care of injured patients are included. While dopamine is considered essential in the Model List, it is listed as desirable in the trauma care guidelines due to the costs associated with training medical and nursing staff in its safe administration via continuous IV infusion. Insulin is included in light of evidence suggesting improved outcomes for severely injured patients with tighter blood glucose control. Additionally, splinting and immobilization are vital methods of pain control for patients with extremity injuries. Similarly, while plain-film radiography is essential at higher hospital levels, portable X-ray capabilities are deemed essential only at tertiary care hospitals. Gram stains are essential at specialist and tertiary hospitals, while tests for electrolytes, arterial blood gases, and serum lactate are desirable but not essential due to cost constraints. Training healthcare providers in trauma care is crucial for implementing these guidelines effectively. Skills such as initial evaluation, resuscitation, and operative management must be emphasized. Continuing education programs, such as Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) and other trauma care courses, have been shown to improve care processes and outcomes. For example, ATLS training in Trinidad significantly reduced mortality rates among severely injured patients. Other courses, such as the National Trauma Management Course (NTMC) in India and the Trauma Team Training (TTT) program in Uganda, are tailored to the specific needs of low-resource settings. Countries should assess which training programs best suit their needs and consider developing national plans to address barriers to training, such as high costs or limited availability.
